orderingVariable: SPECIAL-MORA LOAD, ASCENDING — counting the non-CV morae in each word (long-vowel mora, moraic N, geminate mora; yoon onsets as a half-weight secondary term) — with two explicit subordinate roles: (i) conversational frequency decides MEMBERSHIP of the 180, not order within it; (ii) items 1-41 are position-LOCKED by the week-3/4 grammar's slot requirements and are exempt from the sort. Applied visibly as four tiers: TIER 0 (zero special morae) = items 1-120; TIER 1 = exactly one special mora, ordered by mora type in the sequence moraic N (121-140) -> long vowel (141-160) -> geminate/yoon (161-170); TIER 2 (two special morae in one word) = 171-180. Within every tier the secondary sort is accent-class alternation (see whyThatVariable), the tertiary sort is semantic clustering, and frequency is the tiebreak.
whyThatVariable:
PICK: (d), refined — but "ascending load", NOT "defer the specials".

AGAINST THE STRONGEST RIVAL, (a) pure conversational frequency. Frequency's claim is coverage. But coverage is decided by which 180 nouns you pick, not by what order you drill them in. Every one of these 180 is carded inside 12-18 days at the wk3-5 ramp; by day 20 the learner owns the whole set regardless of internal order, so the coverage delta between position 12 and position 112 is ~zero. What is NOT zero is the encoding quality of item 12: a noun encoded on day 1 with a mis-heard vowel length is a noun that will be mis-heard in running speech for a year, and the SRS will happily maintain the error, because the learner's grading signal is his own faulty percept. Frequency is therefore correctly spent as a GATE (nothing enters the 180 that isn't top-tier conversational) and wasted as a SORT. That is the whole argument: frequency buys coverage, which the ramp gives away free anyway; phonological ordering buys encoding fidelity, which nothing else in the plan buys.

AGAINST (b) mora count. Mora count is a proxy for the thing I actually care about and a bad one. hikooki is 5 morae but only one special (a long o); onna is 3 morae and contains the single hardest early contrast (moraic N before a homorganic nasal). Sorting by length would put onna before hikooki. Sorting by special-mora load puts them in the right order. Where length genuinely matters — a 2-mora word gives the accent contour almost nowhere to sit — I handle it inside the "X ga" frame the plan already mandates, not by sorting on it.

AGAINST (d)-as-usually-stated, i.e. "defer long vowels / geminates / moraic N until the perception block's gains consolidate." This is the version I reject. Perceptual training that is not cashed out in lexical items decays; a category learned in weeks 1-2 on nonsense-syllable minimal pairs and then not met in a real word until week 9 is a category you retrained for nothing. So the specials come in EARLY — tier 1 opens at item 121, roughly day 11 of carding — but METERED: one special mora per word, one mora TYPE at a time, and no word carries two specials until item 171. The perception block's output gets consolidated on live vocabulary while it is still warm, without ever asking the learner to resolve two unfamiliar contrasts in one token.

AGAINST (c) accent class as the sort. Rejected as a sort, adopted as a within-tier constraint, and I take the ACCENTED-LEAD side of the question you posed. Reason: heiban is not a pattern, it is the absence of one, and a learner who meets forty flat nouns first does not learn "heiban" — he learns that Japanese has no pitch, and then never allocates attention to the drop. So the accented drop is installed as a perceptible EVENT first: items 1 and 2 are neko [1] (immediate HL fall) and inu [2] (odaka, fall audible only on the following particle), and heiban does not appear until item 3. Thereafter every block runs roughly 50/50 accented/unaccented with no run of more than three same-class items, so the drop stays a live discriminandum rather than settling into background. Note the odaka trap this creates and that the plan already anticipates: inu [2], kutsu [2], kami [2], heya [2], ie [2], mise [2], mimi [2], ashi [2], niku [2], kome [2], mono [2], yama [2], kawa [2], iro [2], oto [2] and ~15 more are indistinguishable from heiban on the bare word. All of them MUST be recorded in the "X ga" frame or the accent integer on the card is a lie.

AGAINST (e) semantic utterability as the sort. Rejected as a sort because it is not a variable — it is a constraint with a hard edge, and constraints belong in the gate, not the comparator. But it is honoured absolutely: items 1-41 are pinned. And the payoff of that pinning is the finding that made this ordering easy to defend — the entire week-3/4 grammar (copula, kosoado, wa/ga, aru/iru, relational nouns) can be saturated with ZERO special-mora nouns. See notes. So (d) and (e) never actually collide; utterability turned out to select a phonologically clean set on its own.

blocks.label: TIER 0 · POSITION-LOCKED · pointable objects + animates (the kosoado / aru-iru / copula filler set)
items: 1. neko [1] cat — accented lead; clean HL fall on a 2-mora word
2. inu [2] dog — odaka; fall lands on the following particle, teaches the ga-frame's purpose on card 2
3. hito [0] person — first heiban, deliberately AFTER two accented items
blocks.rationale: Position-locked, not frequency-sorted. Items 1-5 are the animate set for iru; 6-14 are the hand-held, pointable set that kore/sore/are must have referents for; 10, 13, 15-19 are the ground nouns that the relational block (21-32) attaches to; 7, 8, 20 are the canonical aru arguments. Every item is 2-4 morae with zero special morae and no voiceless-vowel-devoicing trap except kutsu and tsukue (both flagged for the TTS spec: the u in ku/tsu devoices, and the learner must not encode a deleted mora). Accent alternates deliberately: A A H H H | H A A A H | H H H A A | A H A H H.
blocks.interference: kami [14] paper [2] collides with kami hair [2] (identical accent) and kami god [1] (accent-distinct). Both partners are EXCLUDED from the 180 and deferred to index >=314 under rule S1 (300-index minimum). kagi [7] is a near-neighbour of kaki (persimmon/oyster/fence), which is excluded from the 180 entirely. kasa [8] vs kasa 'bulk' — negligible at beginner level, no action.

blocks.label: TIER 0 · POSITION-LOCKED · relational nouns (hard position: week-3 locative frames cannot run without them) + body
blocks.rationale: The twelve relational nouns are the single hardest-position block in the plan: 'tsukue no ue ni kagi ga arimasu' is the week-3 terminal frame and it is unbuildable without 21-32. Windfall worth stating: all twelve are zero-special-mora, so the hard-position requirement and the phonological sort agree exactly — no exception had to be carved. Body parts follow immediately because they are the other set the learner physically points at, which is what makes kosoado teachable without translation. te [1] and me [1] are 1-mora: acceptable here because their homophone density is low, and the ga-frame gives the contour somewhere to land. This is 21 items rather than 20 to absorb hana (see interference).
blocks.interference: hana [37] is scheduled as NOSE [0], not flower. Deliberate inversion: hana flower [2] is the more 'textbook' word but nose is what the week-4 body-part-plus-kosoado frames need, and only one member can hold an early slot. hana flower is displaced to >=337 (rule S1). Cost accepted and stated: the learner has no word for 'flower' for roughly seven weeks. naka [23] inside [1] collides with naka 'relations' [1] — identical segments AND identical accent, so rule S2 applies: naka 'relations' never receives a bare-audio card at any index and exists only inside the frame 'naka ga ii'. ashi [39] is a proper prefix of ashita [120]; separation 81 is adequate but the ashita card should carry the frame 'ashita no' to block the misparse.

blocks.label: TIER 0 · the house and what is in it
blocks.rationale: Sort is now unconstrained by grammar, so it is pure tier-0 with semantic clustering as tertiary key. This block exists because the week-4 existence-and-location drills need a room's worth of furniture to move things around in, and every one of these survives the 'a beginner actually says it' filter (no zoo animals, no classroom objects — note the absence of enpitsu, kokuban, kyookasho). daidokoro, saifu and the four gairaigo are the first non-wago items in the ledger, at item 48. Note that toire, taoru, doa and naifu are gairaigo with NO special morae — this is why they are here and not in tier 1: gairaigo is not automatically hard, only usually hard.
blocks.interference: kado [46] corner [1] vs kaado (card) [1] — a length minimal pair. Rule S3: short member sits in tier 0, long member is barred from the 180 and enters tier 1 territory later, guaranteeing the short form is already stable when the long one arrives. michi [59] vs mizu [6] — no true collision, but both are /mi/-initial 2-mora heiban-ish; separation 53 is sufficient. fukuro [54] sack vs fukurou (owl) — owl excluded (zoo animal, and a long-vowel partner).

blocks.label: TIER 0 · food, drink, taste
blocks.rationale: Food is the highest-yield concrete domain in real conversation after people and places, and it is unusually clean phonologically in its wago core — note that gohan, pan, ringo, mikan, ninjin ALL carry moraic N and have therefore been held back to 121-140 rather than clustered here. That split is the ordering variable visibly overriding semantic clustering, which is exactly what it should do. mono [79] / tabemono [80] / nomimono [81] close the block as a morphological family, which also front-loads the -mono compounding pattern the learner will meet again in kaimono (78, placed adjacent on purpose).
blocks.interference: hashi [75] chopsticks [1] is the ONLY member of the hashi triplet inside the 180. hashi bridge [2] deferred to >=375 (S1, accent-distinct, admissible later with a disambiguating frame). hashi edge [0] deferred past 1000 or carded phrase-only — it is rare in speech and a third member of a triplet is where S1 stops being enough. kome [67] vs the verbs komu/komeru: no index rule, but the card must be framed 'kome o' since the bare form is a verb stem. sake [71] alcohol [0] vs sake salmon [0] — identical segments, identical accent: rule S2, salmon never gets a bare card.

blocks.label: TIER 0 · outside, weather, time
blocks.rationale: Weather is where beginner small-talk actually happens ('kyoo wa ame desu ne'), so it earns early placement despite offering the densest collision cluster in the whole ledger — four flagged items in ten. Time nouns 96-100 close tier-0's temporal vocabulary; note that kyoo, kinoo and ashita are NOT here: kyoo and kinoo carry long vowels and sit at 141-142, and ashita is at 120. That is the sort splitting an obvious semantic set across a tier boundary, and it is correct: the learner should meet asa/hiru/yoru/kesa clean before spending attention on the kyoo/kinoo vowel length.
blocks.interference: FOUR flagged items. kaze [88] wind [0] vs kaze 'a cold' [0] — identical segments AND accent, rule S2: 'a cold' never receives a bare-audio card at any index and lives only as the phrase card 'kaze o hiku'. ame [89] rain [1] vs ame candy [0] — accent-distinct, rule S1, candy deferred to >=389. kumo [91] cloud [1] vs kumo spider [1] — identical accent, rule S2, spider excluded from bare-audio permanently. tori [92] bird [0] vs toori [146] street [3] — this is a LENGTH pair, not a homophone pair, so S3 governs and the separation is deliberately SMALL (54 indices, ~3 days): the short member must be a stable baseline, and then the long member should arrive close enough that the contrast is felt rather than forgotten. Distance is the wrong medicine for length pairs; ordered proximity is the right one. hoshi [87] star [0] vs the adjective hoshii 'want' [2] — cross-POS length pair, flag for the wk-6 adjective block, no index rule needed here.

blocks.label: TIER 0 · people, self, work, language, colour — closes tier 0
items: 120. ashita [3] tomorrow (approx; [0] also current in Tokyo speech)
blocks.rationale: The humble kinship set (103-108) is placed HERE, 60-80 items ahead of the honorific -san set (175-180), on phonology alone: haha/chichi/ani/ane are zero-special-mora, okaasan/otoosan/oniisan/oneesan carry two specials each. This is a happy accident with real pedagogical value — the learner acquires the humble/own-family register first, which is the register he will actually need to produce, and meets the honorific set later as a systematic derivation from words he already owns. otoko [101] is separated from onna [123] for the same reason: otoko is phonologically clean, onna carries the moraic N. Teaching onna against an already-stable otoko makes the N the only new variable in the card.
blocks.interference: otoko [101] and onna [123] deliberately split across the tier boundary; separation 22 is fine and desirable (contrast pair, S3-like logic). oto [113] sound [2] vs otto husband [1] — a GEMINATE minimal pair. Husband is excluded from the 180 and belongs in the geminate block; when it enters it must sit adjacent-but-after oto, same S3 logic as tori/toori. aka [118] red [1] vs aka 'grime' [1] — S2, grime excluded. ao [119] and aka [118] are the only two colours in the 180; kuro [1], shiro [1], midori [1], kiiro [0] are items 181-184, held out only because 180 is the cap, and shiro additionally collides with shiro 'castle' [0].

blocks.label: TIER 1a · +MORAIC N, exactly one per word, no long vowels, no geminates
blocks.rationale: Moraic N is introduced FIRST among the specials, deliberately, because it is the one special mora whose realisation varies by following segment (hankachi = [ŋ], shinbun = [m], denwa = nasalised vowel, word-final pan = uvular) and therefore needs the longest runway before the learner has to also track length and gemination. The block is ordered by N environment: word-final and pre-pause first (121-131, easiest — the N gets its own full beat with nothing competing), then N before an obstruent (132-140, where the N assimilates and the learner's instinct is to delete it). Every card is a single-N word; no item here also carries a long vowel or geminate. STRUCTURAL FACT worth stating plainly: moraic N is near-diagnostic of Sino-Japanese, so an N block cannot be wago-weighted. I bought the ratio back with seven gairaigo (122, 126-131) rather than by deferring the N block, because deferring it is the mistake argued against in whyThatVariable.
blocks.interference: minna [124] vs mina [0] — same word, colloquial vs formal; card the contracted minna as citation per plan policy, mina only appears inside minasan. shinbun [136] vs shinbun-sha etc, no action. jikan [138] time [K] vs toki [2] time (wago, item 181-190 range) — semantic collision, not phonological; card jikan only in the frame 'jikan ga' to keep the countable/duration sense separate. gohan [121] vs gohan-ya — no action. kaban [125] vs kabin (vase) — one-vowel pair, vase excluded from the 180.

blocks.label: TIER 1b · +LONG VOWEL, exactly one per word
blocks.rationale: Long vowels second. Six wago items lead (141-146) so the contrast is met first in native phonology where the learner has the least interference, then five gairaigo (147-151) where vowel length is the single feature separating the Japanese word from the English one he already knows — koohii/biiru/keeki/chiizu are the highest-value length drills available anywhere in the lexicon precisely because the English source word gives a wrong prior that must be overwritten. Kango closes the block. Note 157 byooin and 158 gakusee: byooin technically carries long-vowel + N and 158 carries long-vowel with the /ei/->[eː] merger; both are flagged as the block's hardest and are the bridge into tier 2. TTS SPEC NOTE: 158 gakusee, 159 tokee, 173 sensee are spelled -ei in kana and MUST be rendered [eː] in audio and doubled-e in the romaji field, or the learner encodes a diphthong that does not exist.
blocks.interference: toori [146] street [3] vs tori [92] bird [0] — the length pair, see block 82-100. Separation 54 is deliberate and small. biiru [148] beer [1] vs biru building [1] — identical accent, pure length pair; biru is EXCLUDED from the 180 and enters no earlier than 400 with an explicit contrast card, because unlike tori/toori the two are also semantically confusable in context ('biru ni ikimasu'). koori [145] ice vs koori 'ward' — ward excluded. kyoo [141] today [1] vs kyoo 'strange/interest' — excluded. ryoori [154] vs ryokoo [156] — both ryo-initial, 2 apart, deliberate: they are not confusable and adjacency reinforces the ryo- yoon onset.

blocks.label: TIER 1c +GEMINATE / YOON (161-170), then TIER 2 · two special morae in one word (171-180)
blocks.rationale: Gemination gets the SMALLEST noun block of the three specials, and that is a finding rather than a compromise: geminate consonants in wago nouns barely exist — Japanese gemination lives in mimetics (chotto, yukkuri, hakkiri), in adverbs, and above all in verb morphology (-tte, -chatta, itte, motte), which the plan already carries in the week 9-10 -te-form block. So the noun ledger can only carry a thin geminate load, and the perception block's gemination training is consolidated by VERBS, not by nouns. Items 161-170 are the honest maximum; 163-168 are gairaigo because that is where beginner-usable noun geminates actually are. Then 171-180 is the first and only tier-2 run: two specials in one word, every item chosen so both specials are of already-trained types. The honorific kinship set closes the ledger as a systematic six-item paradigm derived from words the learner has owned since items 103-108, which makes the two-special load the only new thing on those cards.
blocks.interference: kitte [161] stamp collides with kitte, the -te form of kiru (cut / wear) — a NOUN-vs-INFLECTION collision, the type the plan's contraction-as-citation policy makes unavoidable. Required action is not index separation but framing: card the noun only as 'kitte o' and schedule it to land BEFORE the wk9-10 -te block, so the noun is the stable prior. ojiisan [179] grandfather [2] vs ojisan uncle [0], and obaasan [180] grandmother [2] vs obasan aunt [0]. These VIOLATE rule S3 — the short member should precede the long one, and here the long member goes first. Deliberate exception, defended: the -ii-/-aa- forms are far more frequent as address terms and as reference to non-relatives, and the perception block has by now had ten weeks. uncle and aunt enter at >=380 and MUST arrive as an explicit four-card contrast set, not as isolated items. kooen [172] park vs kooen 'lecture/performance' — both later senses excluded from the 6000's early half. sensee [173] vs sensei-gata etc, no action.

notes: SLOT FILLERS WITH HARD POSITION — the direct answer. Items 1-41 are position-locked and exempt from the sort. By frame: (a) copula 'X wa Y desu' identity/category predicates: hito(3), kodomo(4), tomodachi(5), plus the object set 6-14 for 'kore wa X desu'. (b) kosoado referents — must be small, hand-held, pointable: kagi(7), kasa(8), kutsu(9), hako(10), sara(11), kami(14). (c) wa/ga contrast — needs two same-class contrastable animates: neko(1)/inu(2), and hito(3)/kodomo(4). (d) existence with IRU (animate): neko(1), inu(2), hito(3), kodomo(4), tomodachi(5). (e) existence with ARU (inanimate): mizu(6), kagi(7), kasa(8), tsukue(13), okane(20). (f) locative ground nouns the relational block attaches to: hako(10), tsukue(13), heya(15), ie(16), uchi(17), mise(18), kuruma(19). (g) relational nouns proper, the hardest position in the plan: ue(21) through aida(32), all twelve. (h) body parts for point-and-name kosoado without translation: te(33) through karada(41).

THE FINDING THAT MADE THE ORDERING CHEAP: the entire week-3/4 grammar can be saturated with ZERO special-mora nouns. 'Tsukue no ue ni kagi ga arimasu', 'kore wa kasa desu', 'neko ga imasu ga inu wa imasen', 'heya no naka ni hito ga imasu' — every argument slot fills from items 1-41 and not one of them contains a long vowel, a geminate, or a moraic N. So no exception had to be carved between the utterability constraint (e) and the phonological sort (d). If they HAD collided the honest resolution would have been to pin sensee and gakusee at positions 3-4 and eat the two-special load on day 1; they do not collide, so nothing is pinned out of tier.

COLLISION RULES, stated once and applied throughout. S1 (accent-DISTINCT homophones, e.g. ame rain [1] / ame candy [0]): both may exist in the 6000, minimum separation 300 indices — derived from SRS maturity, not convenience: the second member enters no earlier than the first member's fourth successful review, interval >=21d, which at the 15/day ramp is ~315 cards. S2 (accent-IDENTICAL true homophones, e.g. kaze wind/cold, kumo cloud/spider, naka inside/relations, sake alcohol/salmon): only ONE member ever receives a bare-audio card. The other is carded as a collocation phrase only, permanently. There is no separation that fixes a true homophone; distance just delays the confusion. S3 (LENGTH minimal pairs, e.g. tori/toori, biru/biiru, ojisan/ojiisan, kado/kaado, oto/otto): short member in tier 0, long member in tier 1, which yields separation of ~60 AND the property that matters — the short form is already stable when the long one arrives. Note S3 wants SMALL separation, the opposite of S1. Homophones need distance; length pairs need ordered proximity, because the contrast is the lesson.

ITEMS DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED FROM THE 180 despite being on your flag list: ki, e, ha, hi, chi. All are 1-mora with extreme homophone density (ki = tree/spirit/energy/yellow; e = picture/handle/inlet; ha = tooth/leaf/blade/edge; hi = sun/day/fire/ice). A 1-mora bare-audio card carries almost no accent information even in the ga-frame, and four-way homophony on top of that is unlearnable by ear. These enter later as COLLOCATION cards only: 'ki o tsukeru', 'ha o migaku', 'e o kaku'. I did admit te(33) and me(34), which are also 1-mora, because their homophone density is low. kaki (persimmon/oyster/fence/writing) and kaeru (frog/return/change/buy-back) are excluded for the same reason — kaeru additionally collides with two high-frequency verbs and should never be a noun card.

WAGO:KANGO ACTUAL COUNT, reported rather than asserted. wago 127 (70.6%), kango 32 (17.8%), gairaigo 21 (11.7%). Discounting the four fully naturalised loans that no speaker parses as Sino (gohan, kaban, mikan, ringo) gives functional kango 28 = 15.6%. The 15% target is at ceiling and slightly over, for a structural reason worth recording: moraic N and long vowels are near-diagnostic of Sino-Japanese, so ANY ledger that includes an N block and a long-vowel block runs kango-heavy in those blocks by construction. Items 1-120 run at 2.5% kango; the ratio only degrades from item 121. Since the plan's 85:15 target is stated across the first 1000, the running average stays well inside the envelope.

GAIRAIGO WAS UNSPECIFIED IN THE BRIEF and I allocated 11.7%. Defence: gairaigo is roughly a tenth of conversational noun tokens and cannot be honestly excluded; it is also the phonologically hardest class (koohii, poketto, beddo pile length and gemination onto an English prior that actively fights the correct percept). So gairaigo is concentrated in tiers 1-2 where that difficulty is the lesson — with the four exceptions toire(50), taoru(51), doa(57), naifu(77), which are gairaigo with no special morae and therefore correctly belong in tier 0. Gairaigo is not automatically hard; it is only usually hard.

THE ODAKA TRAP, and why it is an audio-production requirement rather than a card-design one. Roughly 25 items in this ledger are odaka (accent = mora count): inu[2], kutsu[2], kami[2], heya[2], ie[2], mise[2], mimi[2], ashi[2], niku[2], kome[2], shio[2], mono[2], yama[2], kawa[2], tsuki[2], yuki[2], machi[2], hiru[2], oto[2], uta[2], iro[2], gomi[2], nioi[2], kagi[2], te[1], me[1] and others. Every one is acoustically identical to heiban on the bare word. If any of these is recorded bare, the accent integer on the card is unverifiable by the learner and therefore functionally false. All must be in the 'X ga' frame. This is why item 2 is inu: the second card in the entire deck demonstrates why the frame exists.

ACCENT VALUES MARKED (approx) ARE APPROXIMATE and should be checked against NHK Nihongo Hatsuon Akusento Shin-Jiten before TTS generation: chichi[2], ofuro[2], kagami[3], fukuro[3], nioi[2], tabemono[2], nomimono[3], kutsushita[2], ashita[3], densha[0], hankachi[3], koori[0], poketto[2], hikkoshi[0], sakki[1], daidokoro[0]. ashita in particular is [3] in the dictionary and [0] in much of everyday Tokyo speech; pick one and be consistent across the deck rather than recording both. Everything unmarked I am confident in.

THINGS THAT SURPRISED ME. (1) The relational nouns — the block with the hardest positional constraint in the whole plan — are all twelve zero-special-mora. That is luck, and it is the reason (d) and (e) never fought. (2) Gemination has almost no beginner noun vocabulary. I could not honestly fill twenty geminate noun slots without reaching for adverbs and mimetics, which are a different card type. The correct conclusion is not to pad the block but to record that gemination is consolidated by verb morphology in weeks 9-10, and that the noun ledger's job on gemination is only to keep the category alive until then. (3) The humble kinship set is phonologically clean and the honorific set is not, which hands you the pedagogically better order for free — own-family register first, honorific derived later.

WHAT IMMEDIATELY FOLLOWS 180, for continuity: 181 kuro [1] black, 182 shiro [1] white ⚠(vs shiro castle [0]), 183 midori [1] green, 184 kiiro [0] yellow, 185 toshi [2] year, 186 mainichi [1] every-day, 187 kusa [2] grass, 188 ishi [2] stone, 189 ike [2] pond, 190 mori [0] forest. These are tier-0 items displaced only by the 180 cap, not by the sort — the sort's tier-0 pool is larger than 120 and the surplus should be spent here before tier 2 continues.
